questions.question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?

answer.question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?
answer.answer:
The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 a month, and most people pay that standard amount. Two things can make it higher:

1. Higher income. Medicare looks at the modified adjusted gross income reported on your IRS tax return from 2 years ago, and people with higher incomes pay more than the standard amount.
2. A late enrollment penalty. If she doesn't sign up for Part B when she's first eligible, her monthly premium may go up 10% for each full 12-month period she could have had Part B but didn't sign up, and she'd pay that penalty for as long as she has Part B. (She may avoid the penalty if she's allowed to sign up during a Special Enrollment Period or enrolls in a Medicare Savings Program.)

Since she just turned 65, her Initial Enrollment Period is generally the 7-month period that starts 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after — signing up then avoids the penalty. If she gets Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits, the premium is deducted from her monthly benefit payment; otherwise she'll get a bill, usually quarterly.

questions.question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?

answer.question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?
answer.answer:
Based on the handbook's 2026 amounts, here's how it works out for a single benefit period (a benefit period starts when you're admitted as an inpatient and is how Medicare measures this care):

- Hospital, 5 days: he pays the $1,736 Part A deductible, then $0 per day for days 1–60.
- Skilled nursing facility (SNF), 30 days: he doesn't pay the deductible again, because "you don't have to pay the Part A deductible for skilled nursing facility care if you already paid it for care you got in a hospital during the same benefit period." SNF days 1–20 cost $0 each day, and days 21–100 cost $217 each day. Days 21–30 is 10 days × $217 = $2,170.

So for Part A, that's the $1,736 deductible plus $2,170 in SNF daily amounts — about $3,906 total. His 5-day hospital stay also meets Medicare's 3-day minimum inpatient stay requirement for SNF coverage, and the SNF care must be for an illness or injury related to the hospital stay and certified by his doctor.

Separately, if he has Part B, Part B generally covers 80% of the Medicare-approved amount for doctors' services he gets while in the hospital (so he'd owe the rest of that). With Original Medicare and no other coverage, there's no limit on what he pays out of pocket in a year. For his specific bill, he can call 1-800-MEDICARE (TTY 1-877-486-2048) or visit Medicare.gov/coverage/skilled-nursing-facility-care.

questions.question: My mother is having trouble hearing. Does Original Medicare pay for hearing aids, or for the exam to fit them?

answer.question: My mother is having trouble hearing. Does Original Medicare pay for hearing aids, or for the exam to fit them?
answer.answer: No. Original Medicare doesn't cover hearing aids or the exams to fit them — those are on the list of items you'd pay for yourself. It does cover diagnostic hearing and balance (fall risk) exams if a doctor or other health care provider orders them to see if you need medical treatment; your mother can also see an audiologist once every 12 months without an order, but only for non-acute hearing conditions (like hearing loss that occurs over many years) and for diagnostic services related to hearing loss treated with surgically implanted hearing devices. For those covered exams she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, the Part B deductible applies, and there's also a copayment in a hospital outpatient setting. Medicare Advantage Plans and Medicare Cost Plans may cover extra benefits, including hearing services, so a plan may pay for hearing aids where Original Medicare doesn't.

questions.question: I'm 68 and still working at a company with 12 employees, and I have the company health plan as well as Medicare. Which one pays my medical bills first?

answer.question: I'm 68 and still working at a company with 12 employees, and I have the company health plan as well as Medicare. Which one pays my medical bills first?
answer.answer: Medicare pays first in your situation. Because you're 65 or older and your group health plan coverage is based on current employment at an employer with fewer than 20 employees, Medicare is the "primary payer" — it pays up to the limits of its coverage, and your company plan pays second (secondary payer), covering only costs Medicare didn't pay, and it might not pay all of them. One exception: if your small employer is part of a multi-employer plan that includes other employers with 20 or more employees, the group health plan pays first. Since you're still working, the handbook says to contact your employer to find out how its coverage works with Medicare. For more, see Medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/coordination or the booklet "How Medicare Works with Other Insurance," or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY 1-877-486-2048.

questions.question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?

answer.question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?
answer.answer:
Your mom's Initial Enrollment Period (the 7-month window when you first sign up) runs from December through June: it starts 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after it. (Because her birthday isn't on the first of the month, the standard rule applies — the handbook's example: "If you turn 65 on June 2, your 7-month period would begin in March and end in September.")

Coverage start depends on when she signs up:
- If she signs up in the first 3 months (December, January, or February), in most cases her coverage begins the first day of her birthday month — March 1.
- If she signs up in March (the month she turns 65) or in the last 3 months (April, May, or June), her coverage starts the first day of the month after she signs up.

Signing up when she's first eligible is how she avoids a late enrollment penalty. To sign up for Part A and/or Part B, she can visit SSA.gov/medicare/sign-up. Note that for Medicare drug coverage (Part D), a penalty can apply if she enrolls after her Initial Enrollment Period and goes 63 or more days in a row without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage.

questions.question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?

answer.question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?
answer.answer: Because you've had group health coverage based on your husband's current employment, you get a Special Enrollment Period: you can sign up for Part B any time while you're still covered by that group plan, and then during the 8-month period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first. Taking COBRA does not extend that window — COBRA isn't considered coverage based on current employment, so you still have 8 months after the coverage based on current employment ends to sign up for Part B without a penalty, whether or not you choose COBRA, and you generally aren't eligible for another Special Enrollment Period when the COBRA coverage ends. The handbook also warns that if you have COBRA and you're eligible for Medicare, COBRA may only pay a small portion of your medical costs. If you sign up for Part B while your husband is still working and covered, or within the first full month after employer coverage ends, you can ask to delay your Part B start date up to 3 months. You can sign up at SSA.gov/medicare/sign-up.

questions.question: I turn 65 on August 14, I'm still working, and I put money into a health savings account through my job. If I sign up for Medicare during my Initial Enrollment Period, when does my last HSA contribution have to be?

answer.question: I turn 65 on August 14, I'm still working, and I put money into a health savings account through my job. If I sign up for Medicare during my Initial Enrollment Period, when does my last HSA contribution have to be?
answer.answer: If you sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period, the handbook says you can avoid a tax penalty by making your last HSA (health savings account) contribution the month before you turn 65. Since your birthday is August 14 (not the 1st of the month), that means your last contribution would be in July. The reason is that premium-free Part A coverage can go back (retroactively) up to 6 months from when you sign up for Part A or apply for Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits, but no earlier than the first month you're eligible for Medicare — and you can't contribute to an HSA once Medicare coverage begins without a tax penalty.

questions.question: Mom has Original Medicare and nothing else. Is there a cap on what she can be charged out of pocket in a year, and would a Medicare Advantage plan cap it?

answer.question: Mom has Original Medicare and nothing else. Is there a cap on what she can be charged out of pocket in a year, and would a Medicare Advantage plan cap it?
answer.answer:
No — with Original Medicare alone there's no yearly cap. The handbook says "There's no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket, unless you have supplemental coverage—like Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap), Medicaid, employer, retiree, or union coverage." For Part B-covered services she usually pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount (the amount Medicare sets for a covered service) after she meets her deductible.

A Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C) does cap it: plans have a yearly limit on what you pay for covered Medicare services, and that limit may differ for in-network and out-of-network care. Once she reaches her plan's limit, she pays nothing for covered services for the rest of the year. Because of that limit, the handbook notes you don't need to buy supplemental coverage like Medigap — and you can't use Medigap to pay a Medicare Advantage plan's copayments, deductibles, and premiums.

One separate cap does apply if she has Medicare drug coverage (Part D): out-of-pocket costs for Part D drugs are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

answer.question: My mother found a Medicare Advantage plan with a $0 monthly premium. Does that mean she would pay nothing each month for her Medicare?
answer.answer: No. A $0 monthly plan premium only means the plan itself doesn't charge a premium — she would still generally pay her monthly Part B premium (and the Part A premium if she doesn't have premium-free Part A). Some Medicare Advantage Plans do help pay all or part of the Part B premium (sometimes called a "Medicare Part B premium reduction"), so it's worth checking whether this plan does that. Also keep in mind she'd still have other out-of-pocket costs when she gets care, such as copayments and deductibles, and if she has a higher income she may pay an extra amount for drug coverage (Part D IRMAA).

questions.question: My father takes several expensive prescriptions. Is there any cap on what he'll have to pay for his drugs in 2026?

answer.question: My father takes several expensive prescriptions. Is there any cap on what he'll have to pay for his drugs in 2026?
answer.answer: Yes. If your father has Medicare drug coverage (Part D), his yearly out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by his plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Once he reaches that cap, he won't have to pay a copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year. The cap counts his own out-of-pocket spending plus certain payments other people or entities make, including Medicare's Extra Help program. Note that his actual costs before reaching the cap vary with which drugs he takes and whether they're on his plan's list of covered drugs (formulary), the drug's "tier," which benefit phase he's in, which pharmacy he uses, and whether he gets Extra Help. This $2,100 cap applies to Part D drugs; drugs covered under Part B are handled differently (for example, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for certain Part B drugs, and the Part B deductible applies).

questions.question: Dad is 68, has had Medicare since he was 65 and never joined a drug plan because he takes no medication. If he joins one now, will he be charged a penalty, and how is it worked out?

answer.question: Dad is 68, has had Medicare since he was 65 and never joined a drug plan because he takes no medication. If he joins one now, will he be charged a penalty, and how is it worked out?
answer.answer:
Most likely yes. Not taking any medication doesn't exempt him: the handbook specifically says that even if you don't take drugs now, you should consider joining a plan when you're first eligible to avoid a penalty, and you may find a plan with little to no monthly premium. The penalty is generally added to his monthly premium for as long as he has Medicare drug coverage. If he gets Extra Help, he doesn't pay a late enrollment penalty.

questions.question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?

answer.question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?
answer.answer:
The best time is during his Medigap Open Enrollment Period — a 6-month period that begins the first month he has Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance) and is 65 or older. (Some states have additional Open Enrollment Periods.) Medigap is Medicare Supplement Insurance sold by private companies; generally he must have Part A and Part B before he can buy it.

If he waits past that period, he may not be able to buy a Medigap policy at all, or it may cost more. In certain situations he may still have the right to buy one outside that period (called guaranteed issue rights), and some states give additional special rights. Also, if he delays signing up for Part B because he has group health coverage based on his (or his spouse's) current employment, his Medigap Open Enrollment Period won't start until he gets Part B.

To learn more about his rights to buy a policy, he can call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) or his State Insurance Department, or visit Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans to find policies and pricing in his area.

questions.question: Dad signed up for Part B this past January. His doctor's office wants to book him for his annual wellness visit. Is he eligible for that yet, and what will it cost him?

answer.question: Dad signed up for Part B this past January. His doctor's office wants to book him for his annual wellness visit. Is he eligible for that yet, and what will it cost him?
answer.answer: Not yet. The yearly “Wellness” visit — a visit to develop or update a personalized plan to prevent disease or disability, not a physical exam — is available once you've had Part B for longer than 12 months, and your first one can't take place within 12 months of your Part B enrollment. Since your dad's Part B started this past January, he'd need to wait until 12 months after that enrollment. When he is eligible, he pays nothing for the yearly “Wellness” visit if the doctor or other health care provider accepts assignment. But if the provider does additional tests or services that Medicare doesn't cover under this preventive benefit, he may owe a coinsurance and the Part B deductible may apply; for services Medicare doesn't cover at all (like a routine physical exam), he may have to pay the full amount. Medicare covers the visit once every 12 months, and he doesn't need to have had a “Welcome to Medicare” preventive visit first. questions.question: Mom's doctor wants to set up home health care after her hip surgery. What will Medicare charge her for it, and does she have to be bedridden to qualify?

answer.question: Mom's doctor wants to set up home health care after her hip surgery. What will Medicare charge her for it, and does she have to be bedridden to qualify?
answer.answer:
Cost: your mom pays nothing for covered home health services. The one exception is durable medical equipment (like a walker or hospital bed) that Medicare covers as part of her care — for that she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, and the Part B deductible applies.

Being bedridden is not required. She has to be "homebound," which the handbook defines as any of these: she has trouble leaving home without help (a cane, wheelchair, walker, crutches, special transportation, or another person) because of an illness or injury; leaving home isn't recommended because of her condition; or she's normally unable to leave home because it's a major effort.

Two other conditions apply: she must need part-time or intermittent skilled services (skilled nursing care, physical therapy, speech-language pathology, or continued occupational therapy), a doctor or other health care provider (such as a nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant) must assess her face-to-face before certifying that she needs home health services and must order the care, and a Medicare-certified home health agency must provide it.

questions.question: Mom's cancer is terminal and her doctor brought up hospice. Who has to sign off before Medicare will cover it, and what would she have to pay?

answer.question: Mom's cancer is terminal and her doctor brought up hospice. Who has to sign off before Medicare will cover it, and what would she have to pay?
answer.answer:
**Who has to certify:** A hospice doctor and your mom's own doctor (if she has one) must certify that she's terminally ill, meaning a life expectancy of 6 months or less. She also has to sign a statement choosing hospice care (comfort care, also called palliative care) instead of other Medicare-covered treatments meant to cure her terminal illness and related conditions.

**What she'd pay:**
- Nothing for hospice care.
- A copayment of up to $5 per prescription for outpatient drugs for pain and symptom management.
- 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care (care in a Medicare-approved facility so a caregiver can rest — up to 5 days each time).

Medicare won't pay room and board where she lives, unless the hospice medical team decides she needs short-term inpatient care to manage pain and other symptoms. Original Medicare still pays for covered benefits for health problems unrelated to the terminal illness, and hospice is billed to Original Medicare even if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan — she doesn't have to switch back. To find Medicare-approved hospice providers, contact her plan or visit Medicare.gov/care-compare.

questions.question: My parents have Original Medicare. They're going to Portugal in June and to Puerto Rico in October. Would Medicare cover them if one of them ended up in the hospital on either trip?

answer.question: My parents have Original Medicare. They're going to Portugal in June and to Puerto Rico in October. Would Medicare cover them if one of them ended up in the hospital on either trip?
answer.answer:
The two trips are treated differently.

Portugal: Original Medicare generally doesn't cover medical care outside the U.S., so a hospital stay there would generally not be covered. The handbook notes you may be able to buy a Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policy that covers emergency care outside the U.S.

questions.question: Mom spent three nights in the hospital but the billing office says she was under observation the whole time, never admitted. She needs a skilled nursing facility now. Will Part A pay for it?

answer.question: Mom spent three nights in the hospital but the billing office says she was under observation the whole time, never admitted. She needs a skilled nursing facility now. Will Part A pay for it?
answer.answer:
Probably not, based on what the handbook says. Part A covers short-term skilled nursing facility (SNF) care only after "a 3-day minimum medically necessary inpatient hospital stay (not including the day you leave the hospital)" for an illness or injury related to that stay. You're an inpatient only when the hospital formally admits you with a doctor's order; you're an outpatient if you're getting observation services, "even if you spend the night in the hospital." So observation nights generally don't count toward the 3-day inpatient stay.

Two things worth checking:
- If your mom was under observation more than 24 hours, the hospital must give her a "Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice" (MOON), which explains why she's an outpatient and how it affects what she pays for care after she leaves. The handbook also says you now have appeal rights when a hospital changes your status from inpatient to outpatient if you meet certain conditions — see Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/original-medicare.
- The 3-day minimum may not apply if her doctor participates in an Accountable Care Organization (ACO) approved for a Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver, and Medicare Advantage Plans may also waive the 3-day minimum hospital stay — ask her provider or her plan.

questions.question: My father moved to the U.S. at 58 and has only about 6 years of work here. Does he have to pay for Part A, how much in 2026, and what happens if he puts it off?

answer.question: My father moved to the U.S. at 58 and has only about 6 years of work here. Does he have to pay for Part A, how much in 2026, and what happens if he puts it off?
answer.answer:
The handbook says you usually pay no monthly premium for Part A (hospital insurance) if you or your spouse paid Medicare taxes while working for a certain amount of time — "premium-free Part A." If your father isn't eligible for premium-free Part A, he may be able to buy it. If he buys it, the premium in 2026 is "either $311 or $565 each month … depending on how long you or your spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes."

If he isn't eligible for premium-free Part A and doesn't buy it when he's first eligible, his monthly premium may go up 10%, and he'd pay the higher premium for twice the number of years he could have had Part A but didn't sign up (for example, 2 years without signing up means a 10% higher premium for 4 years). Also note that in most cases, if he chooses to buy Part A he must also have Part B and pay monthly premiums for both; if he chooses not to buy Part A, he can still buy Part B if eligible. If he needs help paying the Part A premium, the handbook points to pages 91–92.

The excerpts don't say how many years of work make someone eligible for premium-free Part A or which of the two premium amounts would apply to him — for that, visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE.

questions.question: Mom's only income is her Social Security check and she's struggling to pay her Medicare premiums. Is there a program that would help, and would it do anything for her drug costs?

answer.question: Mom's only income is her Social Security check and she's struggling to pay her Medicare premiums. Is there a program that would help, and would it do anything for her drug costs?
answer.answer:
Yes — there are two programs, and applying for one can start the other.

**Medicare Savings Programs** are state programs that help pay Medicare costs such as your Part B premiums. The handbook says that even if you don't think you qualify, you should still apply: contact your State Medical Assistance (Medicaid) office to get started. For your state's Medicaid phone number, visit Medicaid.gov/about-us/where-can-people-get-help-medicaid-chip or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

**Extra Help** is the program for drug costs. If she has limited income and resources, it helps pay some Medicare drug costs, like premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance, and if she joins a separate Medicare drug plan or a Medicare Advantage Plan with drug coverage, she won't pay a Part D late enrollment penalty. She may qualify if her yearly income and resources are below these 2025 limits: single person — less than $23,475 income and less than $17,600 in resources; married person living with a spouse and no other dependents — less than $31,725 and less than $35,130. In some situations she may qualify even with higher income. Resources count things like checking or savings accounts, stocks, bonds, mutual funds and IRAs, but not her home, car, household items or burial plot.

She qualifies for Extra Help automatically if she has full Medicaid coverage, gets help from her state Medicaid program to pay her Part B premiums and other Medicare costs, or gets Supplemental Security Income (SSI) — Medicare mails a purple letter in that case, and no application is needed. Otherwise she can apply any time at SSA.gov/extrahelp, and that same application can begin the Medicare Savings Program application process; Social Security sends the information to her state unless she tells them not to.

For help with her questions, she can call her State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) — see pages 114–117 or shiphelp.org — or 1-800-MEDICARE (TTY 1-877-486-2048).

questions.question: Mom is in a Medicare Advantage plan and wants to move to a different one for next year. When can she make that change, and when would the new plan kick in?

answer.question: Mom is in a Medicare Advantage plan and wants to move to a different one for next year. When can she make that change, and when would the new plan kick in?
answer.answer:
She has two main chances to switch to a different Medicare Advantage Plan:

1. Open Enrollment Period (the fall period): if the new plan gets her enrollment request by December 7, her new coverage starts January 1.

2. Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31: because she's already in a Medicare Advantage Plan, she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage). She can only make one change during this period, and the change takes effect the first day of the month after the plan gets her request.

Outside those periods she generally can't change plans during the year, unless she qualifies for a Special Enrollment Period (for example, if she moves or loses other insurance coverage) or uses the 5-star Special Enrollment Period (December 8 to November 30 the following year) to switch to a plan with a 5-star quality rating, if one is available in her area.

questions.question: Mom is down to two Medicare Advantage plans, an HMO and a PPO. Would she have to pick a primary care doctor or get referrals, and what happens if she sees a doctor outside the network?

answer.question: Mom is down to two Medicare Advantage plans, an HMO and a PPO. Would she have to pick a primary care doctor or get referrals, and what happens if she sees a doctor outside the network?
answer.answer:
The two plan types work differently:

**HMO:** In most cases she would have to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases she'd need a referral to see a specialist (certain services, like yearly mammogram screenings, don't require a referral). She must get care from providers in the plan's network — except for emergency care, out-of-area urgent care, or temporary out-of-area dialysis, which are covered in or out of network. If she gets non-emergency care outside the network without authorization, she may have to pay the full cost. Some HMOs, called HMO Point-of-Service (HMOPOS) Plans, may let her get some out-of-network services for a higher copayment or coinsurance.

**PPO:** She does not need to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases she doesn't need a referral for a specialist. A PPO has network providers, but she can also use out-of-network providers for covered services, usually for a higher cost, if the provider agrees to treat her and hasn't opted out of Medicare (for Part A and Part B items and services). Emergency and urgent care are always covered, and using "preferred" (in-network) providers saves money.

With either plan it's important to follow the plan's rules, like getting prior approval for a certain service when needed. She can check with the plan or visit Medicare.gov for more information.

questions.question: Dad's drug plan puts his medicine on an expensive tier and his doctor says the cheaper ones won't work for him. Can he ask the plan to charge him less, and how does that work?

answer.question: Dad's drug plan puts his medicine on an expensive tier and his doctor says the cheaper ones won't work for him. Can he ask the plan to charge him less, and how does that work?
answer.answer:
Yes. This is called asking the plan for an "exception." If your dad's drug is on a higher tier and his prescriber (his doctor or other provider legally allowed to write prescriptions) thinks he needs that drug instead of a similar drug in a lower tier, your dad or his prescriber can ask the plan for an exception to get a lower coinsurance or copayment for the higher-tier drug. Specifically, he can ask for an exception if he thinks he should pay less for a higher tier drug because he or his prescriber believe he can't take any of the lower tier drugs for the same condition.

The plan answers with a written "coverage determination" — the first decision the plan (not the pharmacy) makes about his benefits, including how much he pays for a drug; he'll get a coverage determination decision when he asks the plan to make an exception to its rules. For more information, visit Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals- (the handbook's link continues beyond the excerpt), or contact the plan directly.

questions.question: Dad is choosing between Medigap Plan N and a high-deductible Plan G. What extra out-of-pocket costs does each of those carry in 2026?

answer.question: Dad is choosing between Medigap Plan N and a high-deductible Plan G. What extra out-of-pocket costs does each of those carry in 2026?

The handbook's 2026 Medigap chart shows these extra costs:

**Plan N** — Plan N pays 100% of the Part B coinsurance, but you must pay a copayment of up to $20 for some office visits and up to a $50 copayment for emergency room visits that don't result in an inpatient admission. questions.question: Dad has had a Medigap policy for years but wants to try a Medicare Advantage plan. If he hates it, can he get his Medigap policy back?

answer.question: Dad has had a Medigap policy for years but wants to try a Medicare Advantage plan. If he hates it, can he get his Medigap policy back?
answer.answer:
Maybe — it depends on the timing and his situation. Because he already has Medigap (Medicare Supplement Insurance) and would be joining a Medicare Advantage Plan for the first time, the handbook says that if he drops the Medigap policy to join, he gets a single 12-month "trial right period" to get his Medigap policy back once he returns to Original Medicare — but only if the same insurance company still sells it. If it isn't available, he can buy certain Medigap policies, depending on state law and whether he's new to Medicare on or after January 1. Outside that trial right period, he may not be able to get the same policy back, or in some cases any Medigap policy, and he might have to pay more, depending on his state's Medigap enrollment rules and his situation.

Two other points: Medigap policies mostly don't cancel automatically when he joins a Medicare Advantage Plan, so he must contact his insurance company if he wants to cancel — and Medigap can't be used to pay his Medicare Advantage copayments, deductibles, or premiums. For more details on dropping a Medigap policy, the handbook points to Medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/medigap/ready-to-buy/change-policies, and his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) or State Insurance Department can explain his rights to buy a Medigap policy.
